source.title: Unlocking Scaling Law in Industrial Recommendation Systems with a Three-step Paradigm based Large User Model
source.authors: Bencheng Yan; Shilei Liu; Zhiyuan Zeng; Zihao Wang; Yizhen Zhang; Yujin Yuan; Langming Liu; Jiaqi Liu; Di Wang; Wenbo Su; Wang Pengjie; Jian Xu; Bo Zheng

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. There are minor text-extraction artifacts in equations and figures.
record.tranche_reason: The study empirically tests whether scaling trends apply in recommendation systems, using R@10 rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports R@10 scaling results for LUM as model size and sequence length vary. It does not report held-out cross-entropy, token-count or training-compute scaling, small-run extrapolation, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Other performance and efficiency results are not results on the scaling behavior named by the claim. Cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its recommendation model (LUM) at several sizes and reports how R@10 changes with parameter count. That is a new setting (user-behaviour sequence recommendation) with a scale result bearing on V5. The measure is a downstream retrieval metric, not held-out loss. The fitted form is linear in log(P), not a power law in loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that LUM unlocks scaling laws in industrial recommendation: R@10 improves continuously with model size (up to 7B) and with sequence length. They call this a power law, but their fitted equations are linear in log of size or length.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a recommendation-system model and R@10, with model-size and sequence-length sweeps, rather than language-model held-out loss and parameter/token/compute scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 300M parameters, R@10 rises log-linearly with input sequence length from 256 to 8192 (R = 0.0147·log(L) + 0.2326).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recommendation-model retrieval quality improves predictably (log-linearly) with user-behaviour context length.

record.problems: The scaling evidence reported here is R@10 rather than held-out loss. The paper gives fitted equations and figures but no uncertainty estimates for these fits, and does not report compute-optimal allocation or small-run extrapolation.

untested.parts: Held-out loss as the scaled quantity; scaling in training tokens or compute; image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes; uncertainty of the fit.
Language-model held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute: not studied.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.

missing.what: Authors report enlarging baseline DLRMs (DIN, DIEN, SIM, TWIN) gave no further performance gains; no numbers given. This bears on whether scaling holds across recsys architectures.
The individual data points (model sizes and R@10 values) behind the Figure 7(a) fit, including the 7B endpoint mentioned in the abstract.

record.verdict_notes: Industrial recsys paper; the scaling result is a minor section (5.5) next to method, efficiency and A/B results, which are correctly excluded. The 'power-law' label is the authors' own; the reported fit is logarithmic in a bounded recall metric, so it does not match V5's power-law loss form.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or loss-minimising allocation between parameters and tokens.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests recommendation-system R@10 scaling with model size and sequence length; does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other modalities and training regimes.
Does not test predictability of downstream language-model task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting choices or setups for their effects on exponents or compute-optimal allocations, or test bends away from a single power law.

rows.subject: LUM
rows.operation_detail: Trained models at varying model sizes and measured R@10.
rows.note: The authors describe a clear power-law scaling trend; the reported fit is linear in log(P).
rows.check: Subject, value and locator are correct. R@10 rises steadily with model size. However, the fit R = 0.0068·log(P) + 0.1741 is log-linear on a recall metric, not a power law on loss, although the authors call it a power law. The number of sizes, the exact size range (axis log(P) about 12 to 22; abstract says up to 7B) and the token/compute budgets are not given, so the full V5 power-law form cannot be confirmed. Partial, not observed.

rows.subject: LUM
rows.operation_detail: Trained models with varying sequence lengths and measured R@10.
rows.note: The authors describe a clear power-law scaling trend; the reported fit is linear in log(L).
rows.check: This row varies input sequence length (256 to 8192) at a fixed 300M parameters. Context length is not parameters, tokens or compute, so it does not measure the scaling variables the versions name. Move it to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: LUM generative recommendation model on the Taobao industrial dataset, model size varied, R@10 measured
relationships.reason: R1: R@10 improves consistently with size, but only as a log-linear gain in a recall metric, with no loss power law or uncertainty. The text also says baseline DLRMs gain nothing from added size, so scaling depends on architecture in this domain.
relationships.display_finding: R@10 improved consistently and log-linearly with model size, without establishing a loss power law, while baseline DLRMs gained nothing from added size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
